rv.q: If your tear ducts don’t moisten multiple times during this captivating show, you must be missing the empathy gene.

While retaining the jolliness and sentimentality associated with some 170 years’ worth of stage versions (including a competitive flock that opened the year after its publication), Thorne and Warchus have polished the story’s social conscience to a restored brightness.

Still you would need to have a galloping case of the humbugs to dislike the show, which begins on a bare stage, lit with scores of lanterns, as musicians chime carols and actors trawl the aisles, flinging oranges and bags of cookies into the crowd.
This is a Christmas Carol that feels both intimate and epic, a neat trick for a show playing in the cavernous Lyceum Theatre.
This handsome new staging offers a respectable if not revelatory take on the Dickens classic.
Thorne’s interest in father-son dysfunction already swallowed up the Harry Potter plays, now this voracious theme eats A Christmas Carol.
But this import from London’s Old Vic — here starring Campbell Scott — would certainly have Dickens scratching his noggin.
This new musical version of A Christmas Carol is a sumptuous, thoroughly engaging evening that should delight audiences of all ages
Their effortless professionalism adds the spice to this heartwarming treat of a show.

Yes, the play may start off pretty bleak, but by the end, the frantic festiveness of Scott’s Scrooge is so infectious that you leave the theater with a heart so full of joy and light, you’ve all but forgotten the cold darkness of its first half.
The most effective touch by far is the casting of two young actors with cerebral palsy.
But Jack Thorne's retelling breathes new life into the old chestnut, creating an enchanting spectacle that really is something special.
One gets the impression that Thorne invents such dreary business simply so his version of A Christmas Carol is somewhat different than the countless other stage adaptations before it.
